extracted.intended_audience: media studies scholars, communication researchers, and cultural studies students
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and analytic framework for understanding how media messages are produced (encoded), circulated, and interpreted (decoded) by audiences, including social, institutional, technical, and ideological conditions that shape meaning. Useful for analyzing television and other mass-mediated discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of linked moments (production, circulation, distribution/consumption, reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of the process in terms of a structure produced and sustained through the articulation of linked but distinctive moments - production, circulation, distribution/consumption, reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat communication as a complex structure in dominance: each moment has its own modality and conditions of existence and can interrupt or sustain the circuit. Analysis should examine how these moments are connected and how breaks/interruptions occur between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message form as a determinate moment (event must become a 'story')
rubrics_metrics.description: The discursive form of the message has a privileged position in the communicative exchange; a 'raw' historical event cannot be transmitted without being signified within the aural-visual forms of the televisual discourse — the event must become a 'story' before it can become a communicative event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how events are transformed into message form via the formal rules of discourse; recognize that message form is not a random surface moment but a determinate stage requiring integration into wider social relations for effects to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation of codes within discourse (encoding/decoding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meanings and messages appear as sign-vehicles organized, like any language, through the operation of codes within the syntagmatic chain of a discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which codes are employed in encoding and how those codes structure signification; decoding requires the appropriate code competencies and mismatches between codes produce distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production conditions and technical/institutional infrastructure shape encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: At the production end the process requires its material instruments ('means') as well as sets of social (production) relations — the organization and combination of practices within media apparatuses; production is framed by knowledge-in-use, technical skills, professional ideologies, institutional knowledge, assumptions about audience, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how technical infrastructures, professional routines, institutional constraints and relations of production influence the shape and content of encoded messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoding must be translated into social practices to have effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the discourse is received it must be translated into social practices; if no 'meaning' is taken there can be no 'consumption' and, if meaning is not articulated in practice, it has no effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not only what meanings are decoded but how decoded meanings enter (or fail to enter) social practice and produce influence, instruction, persuasion or behavioral outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of symmetry/asymmetry between encoding and decoding (fit of codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The codes of encoding and decoding may not be perfectly equivalent; degrees of symmetry/asymmetry (relations of equivalence) between the positions of 'source' and 'receiver' determine how well meanings are transmitted or distorted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the degree of correspondence between 'meaning structures 1' (encoding) and 'meaning structures 2' (decoding); lack of fit explains systematic distortions and 'misunderstandings' in the communicative exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalization of codes and their cultural specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain codes may be so widely distributed and learned so early that they appear 'naturally' given; visual/iconic signs often seem near-universal, but evidence shows even apparently 'natural' visual codes are culture-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to naturalized codes that conceal coding practices; do not assume apparent 'fidelity' or 'naturalness' means absence of coding—these are ideological effects that must be unpacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation versus connotation and the structured nature of polysemy
rubrics_metrics.description: The denotative level of the televisual sign is fixed by certain codes; its connotative level is more open and can be transformed, exploiting polysemic values — but polysemy is not the same as pluralism and connotative codes are not equal among themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish denotative constraints from connotative openness; analyze which connotations are available, which are preferred, and how cultural/institutional forces privilege some connotations over others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of discourses in dominance and preferred readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourses are mapped into domains hierarchically organized into dominant or preferred meanings; there exists a pattern of 'preferred readings' embedded with institutional/political/ideological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the dominant cultural order, its preferred mappings of social life, and how institutionalized readings channel interpretation; recognize that dominance implies preference and institutional backing rather than total determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive 'work' and reading competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading means not only identifying and decoding signs but the subjective capacity to put them into a creative relation with other signs — a condition for 'complete awareness of one's total environment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audiences' capacities and interpretive practices as socially produced competences rather than purely individualized/private acts; analyze how interpretive work is shaped by broader frameworks of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misunderstandings as systematically distorted communication (beyond selective perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters often complain audiences fail to take intended meanings; this is better conceptualized as 'systematically distorted communication' rather than merely 'selective perception', since patterns of decoding cluster and relate to structural positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique simplistic selective-perception explanations and investigate systematic, patterned deviations in decoding arising from code asymmetries and social positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant-hegemonic decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: When the viewer takes the connoted meaning full and straight and decodes the message in terms of the reference code in which it has been encoded, they are operating inside the dominant/hegemonic position — close to 'perfectly transparent communication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances where decoding reproduces hegemonic meanings; examine professional coding practices that facilitate this 'transparent' reception and the ties between broadcasting professionals and defining elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoding that acknowledges the legitimacy of hegemonic definitions at a general level but adapts or resists them in particular, situational terms — a mixture of adaptive and oppositional elements (negotiated code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for decodings that accept broad hegemonic frames while asserting local exceptions or situated logics; such readings are shot through with contradictions and reflect unequal relations to discourses of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppositional decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoding that globally opposes the dominant framework and retotalizes the message within an alternative framework of reference — an oppositional code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect decodings which reject preferred meanings and reorder signification according to alternative political/moral frameworks; these readings actively subvert hegemonic mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional code's relative autonomy and role in reproducing hegemony
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional code is relatively independent, applying technical and presentational criteria of its own, yet it operates within the hegemony and serves to reproduce dominant definitions (often by apparently neutral, technical practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze professional practices (formatting, personnel selection, staging, presentational norms) and how their 'neutral' technical operations contribute to reproduction of hegemonic meanings—often unconsciously or via structures of access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback loops: circulation and reception feed back into production
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation and reception are reincorporated, via skewed and structured 'feedbacks', into the production process itself; consumption/reception is a moment of production in a larger sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how audience reception and circulation shape subsequent production choices and institutional practices; analyze asymmetries and 'skewed' feedback mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing and attention to social relations/positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses about decoding positions and code correspondences need empirical testing and depend on structural differences of relation and position between broadcasters and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground theoretical claims in empirical audience research; attend to class, institutional, cultural and positional differences that affect encoding/decoding correspondences.
